passages.happening:
‘In that day seven women will take hold of one man’ (verse 1). They tell him they will provide their own bread and their own clothes, if only they may be called by his name and have their disgrace taken away.

The verse finishes the picture of the end of chapter 3, where the city's men fell by the sword and in battle. So many men have died that the women left alive far outnumber them.
passages.hearers:
In ancient Israel a woman without a husband had little economic security and often suffered social disgrace, especially if she had no children. Under normal custom a husband provided his wife's food and clothing. The women of this verse offer to give up those rights and support themselves, asking only for his name, the legal and social standing of marriage.

The first hearers would have understood how far things had fallen. The ordinary protections of their society have broken down, and the women must beg for what was once theirs by right. The verse assumes the aftermath of a war that killed so many men, a scene that fits the Assyrian and Babylonian invasions that devastated Judah over the following century and a half.

This verse belongs with the end of chapter 3. The chapter break here was added later and is not ideal. The verse is not a model of marriage. It is a picture of a ruined society.
passages.later: Lamentations grieves the same kind of loss after Jerusalem fell: ‘We have become fatherless orphans; our mothers are widows’ (Lamentations 5:3).
passages.asks: The women of this verse ask only for a name and an end to their disgrace. Ask who in your community lives with that kind of shame and exposure. And ask what it would mean for a church to be family to them, so that none must beg.

passages.t: The Branch of the LORD, and a holy remnant
passages.happening:
The tone changes. ‘On that day the Branch of the LORD will be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the land will be the pride and glory of Israel’s survivors’ (verse 2).

Whoever is left in Zion and remains in Jerusalem ‘will be called holy’, all who are recorded among the living (verse 3). This will happen ‘when the Lord has washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleansed the bloodstains from the heart of Jerusalem by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of fire’ (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
The phrase on that day has introduced judgment in chapters 2 and 3. Now it introduces salvation. The same day of the LORD that humbles the proud will glorify the remnant.

The word Branch, tsemach, means a sprout, something that springs up from the ground. Here it may mean the growth God gives the land, set beside the fruit of the land. Or it may be a title for a coming king, as it clearly is in Jeremiah and Zechariah.

Being recorded among the living reflects the practice of keeping registers of citizens. Moses speaks of God's book. The survivors are written down as belonging to the city.

The washing is a cleansing of blood and filth, the sins named in chapters 1 and 3. It comes by a spirit of judgment and fire. The first hearers were told that judgment would not be God's last act. He would purify, and what remained would be holy.
passages.later: Jeremiah uses the same word for a coming king: ‘I will raise up for David a righteous Branch’ (Jeremiah 23:5). Zechariah hears God say, ‘I am going to bring My servant, the Branch’ (Zechariah 3:8). And Ezekiel promises, ‘I will also sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean’ (Ezekiel 36:25).
passages.hard:
Is the Branch of the LORD in verse 2 the Messiah, or simply the growth of the land?

Both readings have strong defenders. Those who read it as a title for the Messiah note that tsemach becomes a name for the coming king in Jeremiah and Zechariah, and that the Aramaic Targum, an ancient Jewish paraphrase, renders the verse as the Messiah of the LORD. Those who read it as the land's growth note that the parallel line speaks of the fruit of the land, that Isaiah does not use the word elsewhere as a title, and that the passage is about the remnant and the land rather than a king. A middle view sees an intended double meaning: the renewal of the land and the coming ruler belong together in the prophets' hope.

These notes take no side. The chapter's main point stands on every reading: after judgment, God will give his people beauty, holiness and his presence.
passages.asks: The remnant is made holy by being washed, not by being strong. Ask what God would need to wash away in you. And ask whether you think of holiness as something you achieve or something God gives.

passages.t: Cloud, fire and a shelter over Zion
passages.happening: ‘Then the LORD will create over all of Mount Zion and over her assemblies a cloud of smoke by day and a glowing flame of fire by night’ (verse 5). Over all the glory there will be a canopy, ‘a shelter to give shade from the heat by day, and a refuge and hiding place from the storm and the rain’ (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The cloud by day and fire by night recall the pillar of cloud and fire that led Israel out of Egypt, and the cloud that filled the tabernacle. The first hearers would have heard it at once: the God of the exodus will be present again over his city, not only over one tent but over all of Mount Zion and all its gatherings.

The verb create, bara, is the verb of Genesis 1, used in the Hebrew Bible only with God as its subject. Restored Zion will be a new act of God, not a human achievement.

The canopy, chuppah, is a covering or chamber. Elsewhere in the Bible it is used of a bridal chamber, and in later Jewish custom it became the name of the wedding canopy, though that use comes after Isaiah. Here it is a shelter from sun and storm, God's own glory spread like a roof over his people.
passages.later: God's presence went before Israel in the wilderness ‘in a pillar of cloud to guide their way by day, and in a pillar of fire to give them light by night’ (Exodus 13:21). A psalm promises, ‘The LORD is your keeper; the LORD is the shade on your right hand’ (Psalm 121:5). And Isaiah later calls God ‘a refuge from the storm, a shade from the heat’ (Isaiah 25:4).
passages.asks: God promises shade from the heat and a refuge from the storm. Ask what heat and what storm you need sheltering from now. And ask whether you think of God's presence as something that threatens you or something that covers you.
